---
title: "Worked Examples"
guide-section: "Core Workflows"
---

Seven situations tether is built for, run end to end as one story. Each
section starts where the previous one left the dataset, and ends with
`jj log` and a pointer to the page that explains the mechanics. The dataset
is an Icechunk store `zarr/imaging`, a Lance table `features`, a directory
of raw files `raw/plate1`, and the analysis code repository `code`. (The
Neon database of the other pages is left out, so the story runs locally.)

| Section | Situation |
| --- | --- |
| [1](#reproduce-an-analysis-months-later) | Reproduce an analysis months later |
| [2](#reprocess-on-a-branch-then-land-it-or-throw-it-away) | Reprocess on a branch, then land it or throw it away |
| [3](#ab-two-candidates-keep-one) | A/B: two candidates, keep one |
| [4](#catch-drift-nightly-without-a-watcher) | Catch drift nightly without a watcher |
| [5](#keep-the-data-bill-down) | Keep the data bill down |
| [6](#recover) | Recover from mistakes |
| [7](#publish-history-to-a-registry-experimental) | Publish history to a registry (experimental) |

::: {.callout-note title="Executed, not written"}
`tests/test_use_cases.py` runs every command on this page against local
copies of the objects (and an ephemeral Postgres for section 7). It writes
the command and output blocks you see (`user_guide/_generated/06/`), and CI
fails when a fresh run differs. Ids that change per run are replaced with
stable stand-ins, so the same id means the same thing everywhere on this
page, and the operation log runs on the story's clock.
:::

`jj log` uses a compact template set in the examples' jj config: change id,
commit id, bookmarks, other workspaces' working copies, `(empty)`, and the
description. `@` is this checkout's working copy, `◆` the root. Under git,
read a bookmark as a branch and `@` as `HEAD`.

## 1. Reproduce an analysis months later

*The report is out. Someone asks how a number was computed. The code is in
git; the data it read has moved on three times since.*

Commit the inputs next to the code that read them:

{{< include _generated/06/05-commit.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/05-commit.txt >}}

That commit holds the manifests -- one file per object naming the pin -- and
sits in the same history as `make_report.py`. Months later, from any clone,
the commit id is enough:

{{< include _generated/06/06-open-rev.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/06-open-rev.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/07-open-rev-py.py >}}

`TETHER_REV=695fe286e11b python make_report.py` does the same for a whole
script: every `repo.open()` in it resolves at that commit's pins. And in CI,
so you find out the day a pin stops resolving rather than the day you need it:

{{< include _generated/06/08-verify.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/08-verify.txt >}}

(Under jj, `--all-history` includes the empty working-copy commit on top of
the one you just made; it holds the same manifests, so it verifies the same
pins.)

What tether guaranteed: the Icechunk, Lance and git tags are native refs
their systems will not expire or collect. The raw prefix was *recorded*
(size, count, etag digest), and `verify` says whether it still matches, but
files cannot be pinned; the commit said so.

This commit was made on the trunk bookmark, `main`, where each object's
working ref is its own `main`: the inputs are whatever those branches held.
The commit moved the bookmark with it, and jj opened a fresh empty working
copy on top, as `jj commit` would:

{{< include _generated/06/09-log.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/09-log.txt >}}

Mechanics: [Pinning](03-pinning.qmd).

## 2. Reprocess on a branch, then land it or throw it away

*A new model should relabel the imaging store and rewrite the features table.
Production readers must not see a half-done state, and the attempt may fail.*

{{< include _generated/06/10-new-relabel.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/10-new-relabel.txt >}}

A `relabel-v3` bookmark now sits where `main` is, and every system will get a
branch of the same name. Nothing was created yet: the job opens what it
writes, and the branch for that object appears in its system at that moment,
forked from the pin:

{{< include _generated/06/11-relabel-job.py >}}

`main` -- the bookmark and every system's branch -- is untouched throughout.
When the job is done, commit pins the branches and moves `relabel-v3`. Only
the two objects the job wrote get new pins; `code` and `raw/plate1` are as
the last commit left them:

{{< include _generated/06/12-commit-relabel.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/12-commit-relabel.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/13-diff-relabel.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/13-diff-relabel.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/14-log-relabel.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/14-log-relabel.txt >}}

The bookmark moved; `main` did not. Two endings. Land it:

{{< include _generated/06/15-promote-relabel.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/15-promote-relabel.txt >}}

Nothing moved. Lance refuses, since it cannot move one branch onto another,
and says what to do instead: write the result onto the base branch.
Icechunk *could* have fast-forwarded, and `promote` says so, but holds it:
new labels beside old features on `main` is the half-done state this
exercise exists to avoid
([planned whole or not at all](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#landing-it-tether-promote)).
The two objects the job never opened are skipped.

Landing it by hand is then two steps. Name the system that can move, the
explicit way to land a subset (the trunk bookmark does not move for one):

{{< include _generated/06/16-promote-imaging.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/16-promote-imaging.txt >}}

Then finish the Lance half on the trunk and commit there. Pins are
content-addressed, so the imaging store, now at what `relabel-v3` pinned,
gets the very same pin id, and only `features` gets a new one:

{{< include _generated/06/17-new-main.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/17-new-main.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/18-finish-features.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/19-commit-features.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/19-commit-features.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/20-log-landed.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/20-log-landed.txt >}}

Two lines of history describe the same data now, and the bookmark has done
its job. `drop` throws it away. It is a plan first: the commits only this
bookmark reaches, the bookmark, and what `gc` will release once they are
gone:

{{< include _generated/06/21-drop-relabel-plan.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/21-drop-relabel-plan.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/22-drop-relabel.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/22-drop-relabel.txt >}}

The one pin nothing else names, the Lance version on the branch, is
released (the imaging pin is also `main`'s). Both branches go: Icechunk's
head is `main`'s pin, and Lance's head is a state the dropped commit pinned.
That last rule is
[`drop`'s own](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#throwing-it-away-tether-drop):
`gc --prune-bookmarks` would keep the branch as "unpinned writes".

{{< include _generated/06/23-log-clean.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/23-log-clean.txt >}}

The other ending, a failed attempt, is the same `drop` without the trunk
commit in between. Run from the bookmark itself, it leaves for the trunk
first (`--to` picks another bookmark). `drop` is not undoable by tether, but
[three steps](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#throwing-it-away-tether-drop)
bring a bookmark back.

::: {.callout-note title="Rehearsing a database migration"}
The same flow rehearses a schema change on a Neon database. Run `tether new
-b migration`, apply the migration at the Neon branch's URL, run the tests,
and watch the row counts move with `tether diff main --content`. Neon
cannot promote a child branch, so landing it is the trunk recipe above, or
the migration applied to `main` itself: the branch was the rehearsal.
:::

Mechanics: [Branching and Writing](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#landing-it-tether-promote).

## 3. A/B: two candidates, keep one

*Two labeling approaches. Run both against the same inputs, compare, promote
the winner, and leave nothing of the loser behind.*

Each candidate is a bookmark, `a` and `b`, and each bookmark is a branch of
the same name in every system, so the two never share a branch. Run them
side by side from two checkouts (a jj workspace or git worktree each): **A**
works in `analysis/`, **B** in `analysis-b/`.

**Set up.** B's checkout is created from A's; each starts its own bookmark.
From A:

{{< include _generated/06/24-workspace-add.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/24-workspace-add.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/25-new-a.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/25-new-a.txt >}}

And in B:

{{< include _generated/06/26-new-b.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/26-new-b.txt >}}

**Run and commit.** Each job labels the imaging store through its own
handle. Each `commit` pins its bookmark's branch, lands a dataset commit,
and moves the bookmark onto it. A:

{{< include _generated/06/27-label-a.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/28-commit-a.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/28-commit-a.txt >}}

B:

{{< include _generated/06/29-label-b.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/30-commit-b.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/30-commit-b.txt >}}

Two bookmarks, two lines of history, one fork point -- and the same shape in
the Icechunk store, where `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.a` and `tether.ws.0a1b2c3d.b`
both branch off the snapshot `main` pins. From A, B's working copy shows as
`analysis-b@`:

{{< include _generated/06/31-log-ab.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/31-log-ab.txt >}}

**Compare**, from either checkout, as datasets rather than directories.
Icechunk cannot diff one branch head into another directly, so tether diffs
each against the snapshot they diverged from:

{{< include _generated/06/32-diff-ab.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/32-diff-ab.txt >}}

**Land A.** One command from A. `promote` fast-forwards Icechunk's `main`
onto `a`'s branch and skips the objects A never opened. Everything having
landed, it moves the `main` bookmark onto A's dataset commit.

{{< include _generated/06/33-promote-a.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/33-promote-a.txt >}}

B is untouched: its bookmark and branches are its own. If B's checkout
later moves onto the new `main` (`jj new main`), `tether status` says the
working copy left bookmark `b`, and `tether new b` returns to it.

**Retire B** -- from A's checkout, since B's is about to stop being one.
Forget B's checkout first: `drop` refuses a bookmark another live checkout is
working on, and that is the guard you want. Then drop the bookmark:

{{< include _generated/06/34-forget-b.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/34-forget-b.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/35-drop-b.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/35-drop-b.txt >}}

Nothing is left to run in `analysis-b/`, and the directory can be deleted
(`git worktree remove` already did, for git). B's Icechunk branch went with
the commit that pinned its head, by `drop`'s own rule.

{{< include _generated/06/36-log-final.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/36-log-final.txt >}}

B is gone from history, its pin from the store, and its branch from
Icechunk. `a` and `main` point at the same commit; `jj bookmark delete a` and
a later `gc --prune-bookmarks` retire the winner's branches the same way once
nobody works on them.

Mechanics: [Workspaces and bookmarks](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#workspaces-and-bookmarks),
[`drop`](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#throwing-it-away-tether-drop).

## 4. Catch drift nightly without a watcher

*More inputs across four systems. Some are "immutable" raw files. Something
will change under you eventually, and you would rather hear it from a cron job
than from a wrong result.*

Back on the trunk, register the rest of the inventory -- by hand, or from the
registry or spreadsheet that already lists it -- and commit it:

{{< include _generated/06/37-new-main-4.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/37-new-main-4.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/38-import.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/38-import.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/39-commit-inventory.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/39-commit-inventory.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/40-log-inventory.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/40-log-inventory.txt >}}

Then schedule two commands. `status --snapshot` fingerprints every object
concurrently and only *reports*. On the trunk, `modified` means an upstream
branch moved, and `behind` that a branch-less object's system is past the
pin; both exit 0. `verify` checks that every pin still names what the
manifest says. Each exits 1 when something is wrong: an unreachable object,
a changed immutable file, a pin that does not resolve. On a quiet night:

{{< include _generated/06/41-nightly.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/41-nightly.txt >}}

**A raw file overwritten in place.** The instrument re-exports one well of a
plate registered as `file = "immutable"` (the default). It is the *bytes*
that count, not the timestamp; `status` stops at the snapshot and exits 1:

{{< include _generated/06/42-overwrite.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/43-status-immutable.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/43-status-immutable.txt >}}

That is deliberate: an "immutable" input silently changing is the worst kind
of drift. Either something wrote where it should not have, or -- as here --
the change is legitimate, and accepting it is a re-registration, not a pull:

{{< include _generated/06/44-accept.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/44-accept.txt >}}

**Pins deleted by hand.** Someone "tidies up" the tags in two stores:

{{< include _generated/06/45-delete-tags.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/46-verify-missing.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/46-verify-missing.txt >}}

`repair` recreates every missing pin from its recorded state, while the store
still has that state:

{{< include _generated/06/47-repair.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/47-repair.txt >}}

Lance gets its tag back under the same name. Icechunk never lets a deleted
tag's name be reused, so tether creates the pin under the next
*generation* of the same id, `tether.<id>.2`. The pin id and the manifest
stay, and readers resolve a pin through its live generation, so history
needs no rewriting. `verify` says which one:

{{< include _generated/06/48-verify-repaired.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/48-verify-repaired.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/49-open-after-repair.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/49-open-after-repair.txt >}}

(Between the deletion and the `repair`, reads and forks at that commit
worked too, by the snapshot id the manifest records: a deleted tag does not
make the data unreachable while the store keeps the snapshot.)

**Upstream moves on its own.** A pipeline appends to the Lance table; a
colleague commits to the code repository. On the trunk those branches *are*
the working refs, so `status` sees them as `modified`:

{{< include _generated/06/50-upstream-moves.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/51-code-commit.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/52-status-moved.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/52-status-moved.txt >}}

Nothing watches anything. Each run fingerprints the objects and compares
them with the manifests, one round of metadata calls. Neither command
touches history. To have the dataset *trail* the world rather than watch
it, a nightly `tether pull` on `main` commits whatever moved:

{{< include _generated/06/53-pull.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/53-pull.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/54-log-pull.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/54-log-pull.txt >}}

Mechanics: [Drift](03-pinning.qmd#drift) and [Verify](03-pinning.qmd#verify);
`import` is in [Registries and SQL](10-registries-and-sql.qmd#import).

## 5. Keep the data bill down

*Two weeks of experiments, five commits a day, each pinning a snapshot the
store must now keep. Only the last one matters.*

Decide at `add` time which objects deserve durable pins. The sweep's scratch
table gets `--pin record`: its state is recorded in every commit, but no tag
is created, so the table's own retention decides how long each version lives.
Commit the registration, then run the sweep on its own bookmark:

{{< include _generated/06/55-add-scratch.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/55-add-scratch.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/56-new-sweep.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/56-new-sweep.txt >}}

(A `record` object gets its branch at `new` time, while the recorded
version is known to exist.) Each trial relabels the imaging store and
appends to the scratch table, in `sweep.py`:

{{< include _generated/06/57-sweep-py.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/58-trials.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/58-trials.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/59-log-sweep.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/59-log-sweep.txt >}}

Four Icechunk tags the store must now keep. When the experiment is over, drop
the commits that were only tries and release what only they pinned, in one
step. Later commits keep their manifests exactly as they were (they are
snapshots, not patches), so trial 4 still names its own pins:

{{< include _generated/06/60-abandon-trials.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/60-abandon-trials.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/61-log-abandoned.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/61-log-abandoned.txt >}}

Trial 4 was rebased onto trial 1 (new commit id, same change id, same
manifests), and the `sweep` bookmark followed it. `scratch/embeddings` freed
nothing: it had no pins, which was the point of `--pin record`. (`abandon`
restores each descendant's manifests, so the empty working copy is created
again on top, with a new change id.) Releasing a tag makes the snapshot
*eligible*; the store reclaims the bytes on its own schedule. Recorded
states past their retention show up in `verify --all-history` as missing:
the trade you made with `--pin record`, stated back to you.

**A store that should not outlive its probe** *(experimental)*. So far every
store existed before tether saw it, and tether never deletes what it merely
adopted. A probe often needs a store of its own, such as a second embeddings
table, with no reason to exist once the probe is thrown away. `add --create`
has tether make it, on a bookmark of its own
([Stores tether created](05-reclaiming-storage.qmd#stores-tether-created)).

{{< include _generated/06/62-ls-before.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/62-ls-before.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/63-new-probe.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/63-new-probe.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/64-add-probe.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/64-add-probe.txt >}}

The store is created empty, with an owner marker naming this dataset, and
remembered with the bookmark it was made on in `.jj/repo/tether-created.jsonl`.
On a bookmark its working branch is forked at once, so the first writable
`open` lands on it. (`repo.create("scratch/probe", "icechunk", {"uri": ...})`
does the `add` and the `open` in one call.)

{{< include _generated/06/65-probe-py.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/66-commit-probe.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/66-commit-probe.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/67-status-probe.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/67-status-probe.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/68-log-probe.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/68-log-probe.txt >}}

The probe did not pan out. One `drop`, from the bookmark itself: `--to
sweep` says where to leave for, and `--delete-stores` opts into the
experimental step for the store the probe created:

{{< include _generated/06/69-drop-probe.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/69-drop-probe.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/70-ls-after.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/70-ls-after.txt >}}

Leave, drop the commit, unpin, delete the branches (the sweep table's too:
its recorded state was the dropped commit's), and, with nothing left but
the owner marker, delete the store. The data directory is as it was before
the probe. A store tether *adopted* is never deleted this way, and editing a
manifest cannot make it happen: only the marker in the store and the index
in your repository say a store is tether's to remove. Had another clone
forked its own branch in the store meanwhile, the plan would have kept the
store whole, and said so.

Mechanics: [Reclaiming Storage](05-reclaiming-storage.qmd).

## 6. Recover

*Something went wrong. Three kinds of wrong, and what comes back.*

**An unwanted `new`** -- you started a bookmark you did not mean to, and
`--eager` forked every branch at once. The op log knows what was created:

{{< include _generated/06/71-new-scratch.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/71-new-scratch.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/72-ops.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/72-ops.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/73-undo-new.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/73-undo-new.txt >}}

Five branches deleted, the workspace file and the VCS working copy put back,
the bookmark gone: the checkout is on `sweep` again as if nothing happened.
`sweep`'s own branches were never in play, since a new bookmark forks its
own.

**One object's branch on the wrong state** -- everything else is fine, only
`zarr/imaging` should go back to what an older commit pinned. `restore`
resets the current bookmark's branch for that object, and nothing else:

{{< include _generated/06/74-restore.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/74-restore.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/75-status-restored.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/75-status-restored.txt >}}

The other branches, the manifests and the working copy stay put, and the
next `commit` would pin what you restored. Here it was a demonstration.
`undo` does not guess where a branch it *reset* should go, so it restores
the workspace record, says what the branch was, and leaves the move to you:

{{< include _generated/06/76-undo-restore.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/76-undo-restore.txt >}}

`restore` is its own undo: name the commit whose state you want. The branch
holds the demonstration's state, which this workspace never committed, so
`restore` asks for `--discard` before it throws that away:

{{< include _generated/06/77-restore-back.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/77-restore-back.txt >}}

**Several things in a row.** A restore you did not mean, then a bookmark you
did not mean. `undo` reverses the newest operation each time; run it once
per slip:

{{< include _generated/06/78-restore-features.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/78-restore-features.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/79-new-again.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/79-new-again.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/80-ops-again.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/80-ops-again.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/81-undo-again.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/81-undo-again.txt >}}

{{< include _generated/06/82-undo-restore-features.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/82-undo-restore-features.txt >}}

The restore had *created* `features`' branch on `sweep` (nothing had written
to `features` there yet), so undoing it deletes that branch again, and
`sweep` has exactly the branches it had before.

**A pin deleted by hand, or by a `gc` run on the wrong clone**: the
manifests still promise it, and section 4 ran this one. `verify` reports
`missing`, and `repair` recreates the pin from the recorded state; until
then, reads and forks at that commit fall back to the recorded snapshot.

None of this touched history: the `scratch` and `again` bookmarks came and
went without a commit, and `restore` acts on the stores. The log is what
section 5 left, and the workspace is back on `sweep`:

{{< include _generated/06/83-log-recovered.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/83-log-recovered.txt >}}

tether's `undo` and `repair` cover tether's side, and say exactly what they
could not do (a snapshot the store already expired, a `promote`); `jj undo`
covers the VCS's ([Undo](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#undo)).

Mechanics: [`ops`, `undo`, `repair`](07-cli.qmd#ops-undo-repair) in the CLI Guide.

## 7. Publish history to a registry (experimental)

*A dashboard, a training pipeline, and a data catalog all want to know which
state of which table a run used. None of them should have to clone the
repository to find out.*

Push the history into Postgres -- after every commit to `main`, typically
from CI. Every commit on every bookmark goes, with its parents, refs, and
one row per object per commit:

{{< include _generated/06/84-publish.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/84-publish.txt >}}

Consumers join their own run log against `tether.objects` -- the per-commit
table; `tether.object_states` is the distinct (system, state) pairs a
catalog keys on. A training run recorded which dataset commit it read, and
the join says what that meant for every input:

{{< include _generated/06/85-consumer-join.py >}}

{{< include _generated/06/85-consumer-join.txt >}}

`pin_id` is null for the recorded-only objects (the raw plates, the
`--pin record` scratch table); their `state_json` is still the exact state.
For a provenance dashboard, `tether export` writes the same tables as files:

{{< include _generated/06/86-export.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/86-export.txt >}}

When the registry, not the repository, is where objects are declared, run
the other direction: `tether import` from a query, then `commit`. Section 4
did that from a CSV.

Producers and consumers meet in the middle. The producer commits and
publishes. The consumer's pipeline verifies the commit it is about to read,
and refuses to start on a pin that is gone (`--deep` opens each recorded
state, the only way to check a `record`-pinned object):

{{< include _generated/06/87-verify-rev.sh >}}

{{< include _generated/06/87-verify-rev.txt >}}

`publish` and `export` do not write to the repository, so the story ends
where section 5 left it: the sweep on its bookmark, `main` behind it.
Landing it is section 2's recipe. `promote` will refuse the Lance scratch
table and hold the imaging store, so `promote zarr/imaging` lands the labels
on purpose, and the scratch rows stay on their branch.
